rule_link.how_it_backs: Justifies the cadence-ladder drill and fair/critical knee scores for overstriding runners: a small (+5 to +10%) step-rate increase at the same speed substantially lowers hip and knee joint loading, so the knees rule treats low-cadence overstride as a trainable loading flaw.

summary: Heiderscheit and colleagues tested how changing step rate alters lower-limb joint mechanics during running. Runners ran at their preferred step rate and at slightly higher and lower rates while speed was held constant. Even subtle step-rate increases meaningfully reduced loading at the hip and knee joints. The authors conclude that raising step rate is a practical lever for cutting joint loading and possibly injury risk.
methods_signal: Within-subject experiment in healthy recreational runners: preferred step rate manipulated up and down by small percentages at constant treadmill speed, with 3D hip/knee/ankle joint kinetics.

snippet.text: Nudge cadence up ~5-10% at the same pace and the hips and knees carry meaningfully less load — small step-rate fixes buy large joint-load savings.
snippet.grounds_in: Paraphrase of Abstract + Conclusion (joint-loading reduction with increased step rate)

figure.what_it_shows: Schematic dose-response: cadence axis (preferred, +5%, +10%) against relative hip/knee loading bars trending down as step rate rises.
